title: A sponsored trip
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in orthopaedics, hoping to apply for surgical training. A representative from an implant company offers to pay for your travel and registration at an international conference.

The condition is that you attend a half-day workshop promoting the company's new hip implant.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Check the trust's policy on sponsorship.
options.brief: Trusts have rules on accepting industry funding.
options.detailed: Most trusts have policies on sponsorship and conflicts of interest. Checking it is the first step.

options.text: Accept, as you don't choose implants as an F2.
options.brief: Your future influence and perceived conflict still matter.
options.detailed: You may influence choices later, and the arrangement could still be seen as an inducement.

options.text: Accept, and declare it on the trust's register.
options.brief: Declaring helps, but the conditional nature is the problem.
options.detailed: Declaration is good practice for acceptable sponsorship, but a condition tied to product promotion is what makes this inappropriate.

options.text: Accept, but skip the workshop once you're there.
options.detailed: This breaks the agreement and is dishonest.

options.text: Decline funding that depends on attending their promotion.
options.brief: Conditional funding creates a conflict of interest.
options.detailed: Accepting funding on condition that you attend promotion could influence, or appear to influence, your judgement about their products.

options.text: Ask your supervisor about study leave funding instead.
options.brief: A legitimate way to fund the conference.
options.detailed: Study budgets may cover some or all of the cost, without any conflict of interest.

options.text: Report the representative to the company.
options.detailed: The offer may be common practice. Declining is enough.

options.text: Ask colleagues whether they have accepted similar offers before.
options.brief: Others' choices don't make it appropriate.
options.detailed: What others have done doesn't change your own obligations.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you recognise and avoid a conflict of interest created by conditional industry funding.
explanation.keyDetails: The funding is conditional on attending product promotion. You are early in your career. Legitimate funding may be available.
explanation.reasoning: [A] checks the rules, [E] declines the conditional funding, and [F] looks for legitimate funding. The distractors accept it ([B], [C]), are dishonest ([D]), overreact ([G]), or follow others ([H]).
explanation.competing: [C] is the closest call: declaring sponsorship is good practice. The condition tied to promotion is what makes this unacceptable.

references.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest
